title: Gospel of John: The Road to Easter
intro: 47 days through the Gospel of John, from Ash Wednesday to Easter Sunday, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Today is Ash Wednesday, when many Christians receive a cross of ashes on the forehead. In Western churches it begins Lent, the 40 days before Easter, not counting Sundays; Orthodox Easter often falls later. Starting today, 47 days through the Gospel of John, ending at the empty tomb on Easter Sunday. John opens by echoing Genesis 1:1, and "Word" translates the Greek logos, which could also mean reason or message.

John's opening lines, often called the Prologue, introduce themes that run through the whole book, like light and darkness. The Greek verb translated "overcome" can also mean "grasp," which is why the King James Version reads "the darkness comprehended it not." Tradition credits this Gospel to the apostle John, and many scholars think it was the last of the four, written late in the first century.

The Word who was with God in the beginning now becomes a human being. "Made His dwelling" literally means "pitched His tent" in Greek, recalling the tabernacle, the tent where God's presence dwelt among Israel in the wilderness. Christians call this the Incarnation, from Latin words meaning "in flesh."

John the Baptist sees Jesus coming. (This Gospel simply calls him John, and its author never gives his own name.) Lambs were offered in the temple every day and eaten at Passover, the festival remembering Israel's escape from slavery in Egypt. That Passover image returns at the end of John's story.

Philip tells Nathanael that they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about: Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael is skeptical. Nazareth was a small village in Galilee, never mentioned in the Hebrew scriptures. Philip's reply repeats Jesus' own invitation a few verses earlier: "Come and see."

At a wedding in Cana in Galilee, the wine runs out, an embarrassment for the hosts. Jesus' mother, never called Mary in John's Gospel, turns to the servants. At Jesus' word, six stone jars holding 20 to 30 gallons each are filled with water, and it becomes better wine than what was served first. Only John tells this story, and he calls it the first of Jesus' "signs": acts that point to who he is.

Jesus drives the merchants and money changers out of the temple courts, and the authorities demand a sign to prove his authority. John explains that Jesus was speaking about his own body. Mark places this scene in Jesus' last week; John puts it near the start. Scholars debate whether it happened twice or John arranged his story by theme.

Nicodemus, a Pharisee and a leader among his people, comes to Jesus at night. The Greek word translated "again," anothen, can also mean "from above." Nicodemus hears only the first meaning and asks how a grown man could be born a second time. He appears only in John, and he will be back.

Jesus is still talking with Nicodemus, and he uses a play on words. In Greek, pneuma means both "wind" and "spirit," and so does the Hebrew word ruach. Wind can't be seen, only heard and felt, and Jesus compares new birth by the Spirit to it.

Often called the best-known verse in the Bible. The Greek word translated "so" mainly means "in this way," pointing to how God loved: by giving. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks, so translations differ on whether these are still Jesus' words to Nicodemus or the Gospel writer's own reflection.

John the Baptist's followers are worried that the crowds are now going to Jesus instead. John compares himself to the friend of the bridegroom, something like a best man, glad to step aside. Augustine later tied this verse to the calendar: the Baptist's birth is celebrated in June, as days begin to shorten, and Jesus' in December, as they begin to lengthen.

Passing through Samaria, a tired Jesus sits by Jacob's well around noon and asks a local woman for a drink. Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility over who were Israel's true heirs and where God should be worshiped, Jerusalem or Mount Gerizim in Samaria. A Jewish teacher asking a Samaritan woman for a drink crossed two lines at once.

Jesus has offered the woman "living water," which in everyday speech meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern. She takes him literally at first. The prophet Jeremiah had called God "the fountain of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13), an image Jesus' listeners may have recognized.

Jesus tells the woman things about her past and says he is the Messiah. She leaves her water jar and goes back to town with this question, and many there come to believe, calling him "the Savior of the world." Eastern Orthodox tradition gives her the name Photini, "the enlightened one," and honors her as a saint.

Back in Cana, a royal official, probably in the service of Herod Antipas, begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son in Capernaum. Jesus sends him home with these words instead. On the way, his servants meet him with news that the boy recovered at the very hour Jesus spoke. John counts this as the second sign.

At a feast in Jerusalem, Jesus meets a man who has been an invalid for 38 years, lying by the Pool of Bethesda. Archaeologists have uncovered a large double pool near St. Anne's Church in the Old City that many identify as this one. Many Bibles skip verse 4, which is missing from the oldest manuscripts and was likely added later to explain the stirring of the water.

Criticized for healing on the Sabbath, Jesus answers with a long speech, one of many in John, which has far fewer parables than Mark. "Truly, truly" is the Hebrew word amen said twice. Only John doubles it, about 25 times, to mark an especially solemn statement.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, told in all four Gospels. Only John mentions the boy, pointed out by the disciple Andrew, and that his loaves were barley, the cheaper bread of ordinary people. John also notes that Passover was near, one of three Passovers he mentions, which is one reason tradition says Jesus' ministry lasted about three years.

That night the disciples are rowing across the Sea of Galilee in a strong wind when they see Jesus walking toward them on the water. "It is I" is literally "I am" in Greek, ego eimi. Many readers hear an echo of the name God gave Moses at the burning bush: "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14).

The day after the feeding, the crowd asks for a sign like the manna, the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the wilderness. Jesus answers with the first of seven "I am" sayings in John, each pairing "I am" with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, and vine. None of these sayings appears in Mark.

After the bread of life teaching, many followers find it too hard to accept and leave. Jesus asks the Twelve whether they want to go too, and Peter answers for them. Many scholars see this as John's counterpart to Peter's declaration in Mark 8, "You are the Christ."

Jesus goes to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles; John notes that even his own brothers did not believe in him. Teaching in the temple, he defends his Sabbath healing: boys were circumcised on the Sabbath when their eighth day fell on it, so why not make a whole person well? This is his conclusion.

Tabernacles was the autumn harvest festival, when people lived in temporary shelters to remember Israel's years in the wilderness. According to the Mishnah, an early Jewish law code, priests poured out water from the Pool of Siloam at the temple altar each day of the feast. On the last and greatest day, Jesus stands and calls out this invitation.

The chief priests and Pharisees had sent temple officers to arrest Jesus. They come back empty-handed, with this explanation. Then Nicodemus, the Pharisee who once visited Jesus at night, speaks up, asking whether their law condemns a man without first hearing him.

Religious leaders bring a woman caught in adultery and ask whether she should be stoned, hoping to trap Jesus. He writes on the ground; the story never says what. This story is missing from the oldest manuscripts of John, so many Bibles bracket it; many scholars think it's an early story about Jesus that copyists added later.

The second of John's "I am" sayings, spoken in the temple near the treasury. The Mishnah describes giant lamps lit in that part of the temple during the Feast of Tabernacles, bright enough to light up all of Jerusalem. Many scholars think Jesus' words play on that setting.

His listeners object that, as Abraham's descendants, they have never been anyone's slaves, and Jesus explains that he means slavery to sin. The line about truth is carved in the lobby of CIA headquarters, and its Latin form, Veritas vos liberabit, is the motto of Johns Hopkins University.

The argument about Abraham ends here. Jesus says "I am," not "I was," and many readers hear God's name from Exodus 3:14 once more. The crowd seems to take it as a claim to be divine: in the next verse they pick up stones to throw at him, the penalty for blasphemy in the law of Moses.

Seeing a man blind from birth, the disciples ask whose sin caused it, a common assumption at the time. Jesus answers that neither the man nor his parents sinned, then puts mud on his eyes and sends him to wash in this pool. In 2004, workers repairing a sewer line in Jerusalem uncovered steps of the Siloam pool from Jesus' time.

Religious leaders question the healed man, insisting that Jesus is a sinner for healing on the Sabbath. He sticks to what he knows, and they end up throwing him out. John Newton, a former slave-ship captain, echoed this line in his hymn "Amazing Grace": "was blind, but now I see."

Jesus is still speaking to the leaders who threw out the healed man. The chapter numbers we use date only from the 1200s, so the shepherd speech follows straight on from that scene. "Fullness" translates a Greek word for abundance, more than enough; the King James Version has "more abundantly."

The fourth "I am" saying (the third was "I am the gate"). In the Hebrew scriptures, God is Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23), and the prophet Ezekiel condemned leaders who fed themselves instead of the flock. Some of the earliest Christian art, painted in the catacombs of Rome, shows Jesus as a young shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders.

It's winter, and Jesus is at the temple for the Feast of Dedication, known today as Hanukkah. It celebrated the rededication of the temple around 164 BC after the Greek king Antiochus IV defiled it, and this is its only mention in the New Testament. Asked to say plainly whether he is the Messiah, Jesus answers with this, and the crowd picks up stones again.

Word comes that Jesus' friend Lazarus is sick in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem, yet Jesus waits two days before setting out. By the time he arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and his sister Martha goes out to meet him with these words. A few verses later, her sister Mary greets Jesus with the very same words.

Jesus tells Martha that her brother will rise again, and she answers that she knows he will, in the resurrection at the end of time. Jesus replies with the fifth "I am" saying. These words open the funeral service in the Book of Common Prayer and are read at many Christian funerals.

The shortest verse in most English Bibles. Mary has fallen at Jesus' feet weeping, and the mourners with her are wailing. For Jesus, John switches to a different Greek word, one that means shedding tears rather than loud mourning. He grieves even though, in John's telling, he is about to raise Lazarus.

Lazarus has been in the tomb four days, and Martha warns about the smell when Jesus asks for the stone to be removed. After a prayer, he calls out, and the dead man walks out wrapped in burial cloths. Lazarus is the Greek form of Eleazar, "God has helped." Eastern Orthodox churches remember this story on Lazarus Saturday, the day before Palm Sunday.

News of Lazarus reaches the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, which fears a popular movement will bring Roman force down on the nation. The high priest Caiaphas offers this cold calculation, and John reads it as an unintended prophecy. In Mark, the chief priests' plot follows the temple scene; in John, it follows Lazarus.

Six days before Passover, Jesus is back in Bethany at a dinner with Martha, Mary, and Lazarus. Nard was a perfume imported from the Himalayas, and Judas complains it was worth 300 denarii, about a year's wages for a laborer. Mark tells a similar story about an unnamed woman. In John, the next day is the entry into Jerusalem, and tomorrow is Palm Sunday.

Today is Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week. Crowds in Jerusalem for Passover wave palm branches, a symbol of victory, as Jesus rides in on a young donkey. "Hosanna" is Hebrew for "save, please," from Psalm 118. Only John mentions palms, which is where this Sunday gets its name.

Monday of Holy Week. Some Greeks who have come for Passover ask to see Jesus, and he replies that the hour has come. All through John, his "hour" had not yet come; now it has, and he describes his death with the image of a seed. Dostoevsky chose this verse as the epigraph for The Brothers Karamazov.

Tuesday of Holy Week. John devotes chapters 13 to 17 to Jesus' last evening with his disciples, a long farewell found only in his Gospel. This plan reads from it through Thursday, saving the foot washing that opens it for last. Thomas has just asked how they can know the way; this is the sixth "I am" saying. The earliest Christians called their movement "the Way" (Acts 9:2).

Wednesday of Holy Week, known in some traditions as Spy Wednesday, recalling Judas' secret deal to betray Jesus. In the farewell speech, Jesus has just called himself the true vine and his disciples the branches, the last of the seven "I am" sayings. This verse is carved on many war memorials.

Today is Maundy Thursday, the night John 13 to 17 took place. Unlike Mark, John doesn't describe the bread and cup at the Last Supper; instead he tells how Jesus washed his disciples' feet, a task usually left to servants. "Maundy" comes from the Latin mandatum, "commandment," after the new commandment Jesus gives later that night: love one another.

Today is Good Friday, when Christians remember the crucifixion. "It is finished" is a single word in Greek, tetelestai: completed, accomplished. In Mark the Last Supper is a Passover meal, but in John, Jesus dies on the day before Passover, the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, recalling John the Baptist's words: "Look, the Lamb of God."

Today is Holy Saturday, the quiet day between the cross and Easter. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who first came to Jesus by night, wrap his body in linen with about 75 pounds of myrrh and aloes, a lavish amount. With the Sabbath about to begin, they lay him in this nearby tomb. Many churches hold an Easter Vigil after dark tonight.

Today is Easter Sunday. Weeping outside the empty tomb, Mary Magdalene mistakes Jesus for the gardener until he says her name. Because she is the first to announce the resurrection, Christian tradition calls her the "apostle to the apostles." That's the road to Easter through the Gospel of John. Thank you for walking it with me.
